[[Shah Waliullah Dehlawi]] | influenced = }} '''Al-Murtaḍá al-Husaynī al-Zabīdī''' ({{langx|ar|المرتضى الحسيني الزبيدي}}), or '''Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Murtaḍá al-Zabīdī''' (1732–1790 / 1145–1205 [[Islamic calendar|AH]]), also known as '''Murtada al-Zabidi''', was an [[Indian people|Indian]] [[Sunni]] [[polymath]] based in [[Cairo]].{{cite book |author=Jens Hanssen, Amal N. Ghazal |title=The Oxford Handbook of Contemporary Middle-Eastern and North African History|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|date=11 November 2020|isbn=978-0-19-967253-0|page=47}} He was a [[Hanafi]] scholar, [[Muhaddith|hadith specialist]], [[philologist]], [[linguist]], [[lexicographer]], [[genealogist]], [[biographer]], [[historian]], [[sufi|mystic]] and [[Kalam|theologian]].{{cite journal|title=The World of Murtada Al-Zabidi (1732-91) Life, Networks and Writings|first=Stefan |last=Reichmuth|jstor=23265818|journal=The Arab Studies Journal|volume=19 |issue=1|date=2011|pages=142–146}}{{cite book |last1=Martin |first1=B. G. |title=Muslim Brotherhoods in Nineteenth-Century Africa|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|date=13 February 2003|isbn=978-0-521-53451-2|page=48}}{{cite book |author=[[Nelly Hanna]], [[Raouf Abbas]]|title=Society and Economy in Egypt and the Eastern Mediterranean, 1600-1900 Essays in Honor of André Raymond|publisher=[[American University in Cairo Press]]|date=November 2005|isbn=978-1-61797-240-9|page=}} He was considered one of the leading intellectuals of the 18th century.{{cite book |last1=Esposito |first1=John L. |author-link=John Esposito|title=The Oxford History of Islam|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|date=27 December 1999|isbn=978-0-19-988041-6|page=}} He was also regarded as the greatest Hadith scholar of his time and one of the foremost [[Philology|philologists]] of the [[Islamic Golden Age|Arab post-classical era]].{{cite book |last1=Voll |first1=John O. |author-link=John Obert Voll|title=Islam Continuity and Change in the Modern World, Second Edition|publisher=[[Syracuse University Press]]|date=December 1994|isbn=978-0-8156-2639-8|page=61}}{{Cite book |last=Reichmuth |first=Stefan |author-link=Stefan Reichmuth (academic) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UYaCBAAAQBAJ |title=The World of Murtada Al-Zabidi: 1732-91 Life, Networks and Writings |date=2009-05-04 |publisher=Gibb Memorial Trust |isbn=9781909724723 |pages=54–59 |language=en}} ==Biography== Murtaḍá was born in 1732 (1145AH) in [[Bilgram]], Hardoi, Uttar Pradesh, India. His family originated from [[Wasit, Iraq|Wasit]] in [[Iraq]], from where his parents had emigrated to the [[Hadramawt]] region in the east of [[Yemen]]{{snd}}where the Husaynī tribe is situated. Murtaḍá earned his [[Nisba (onomastics)|nisba]] 'al-Zabīdī' from [[Zabīd]] in the south western coastal plains of Yemen, which was a centre of academic learning where he had spent time studying. He began studying [[Hadith studies|Hadith]] in [[Delhi]] under the most prominent scholar of his time, [[Shah Waliullah Dehlawi]].{{cite book |last1=Robinson |first1=Francis |author-link=Francis Robinson|title=The 'Ulama of Farangi Mahall and Islamic Culture in South Asia|publisher=[[C. Hurst & Co.|C. Hurst]]|date=2001|isbn=978-1-85065-475-9|page=225}} He travelled to [[Hejaz]] ([[Jeddah]], [[Mecca]] and [[Madinah]]) and then settled in [[Egypt]]. He was renowned in the Islamic world. Rulers from [[Hejaz]], [[India]], [[Yemen]], [[Levant]], [[Iraq]], [[Morocco]], [[Turkey]], [[Sudan]] and [[Algiers]] corresponded with him; people sent him presents and gifts from everywhere. He was revered and admired so much that some people in Western Africa believed that their [[Hajj]] was incomplete if they did not plan to see Murtađa Zabīdī. He died in [[Cairo]] during an epidemic plague in the year 1205 AH/1790 CE.{{cite web|url=http://attahawi.com/2011/07/14/imam-sayyid-murtada-al-zabidi/|title=MUSLIM BIBLIOPHILIA: Imam Sayyid Murtada al-Zabidi|language=Arabic|website=attahawi.com|date=14 July 2011 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140707082420/http://attahawi.com/2011/07/14/imam-sayyid-murtada-al-zabidi/|archive-date=7 July 2014}} ==Reception== [[Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Kattani|Al-Kattānī]] states in his book'' Fahris al-Fahāris'': “Zabīdī was peerless in his time and age. None after [[Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani|Ibn al-Ĥajar al-Ásqalāni]] and his students can match Az-Zabīdī in terms of his encyclopaedic knowledge of (Prophetic) traditions and its associated sciences; nor in fame or list of students.” Zabidi's immense proficiency of diverse sciences and his thriving trade with books as well as with his own writings was described with commendation by one of his Maghribi visitors, Ibn 'Abdal al-Salam al-Nasiri:{{cite book |last1=Reichmuth |first1=Stefan |author-link=Stefan Reichmuth (academic)|title=The World of Murtada Al-Zabidi (1732-91) Life, Networks and Writings|publisher=[[Gibb Memorial Trust]]|date=2009|isbn=978-0-906094-60-0|page=72}} {{bquote|He was master of [Collections of] hadith, tafsir, Arabic lexigraphy and other diverse sciences, unequalled by any of those scholars whom we met in the East or West [...] You find him continuously buying and copying against payment, borrowing books from remote regions, other books being sent to him as presents. Apart from that he makes gifts and donations. [...] He is a highly prolific author. By Allah (God), he is indeed the [[Al-Suyuti|Suyuti]] of his time, like Suyuti himself or Ibn Sahin and Ibn Hajar far beyond ordinary men. (Even) if those came together with him, they would surely admit that superiority is not with the first ones (al-Fadila lam tankin li'l-uwal).}} ==Works== As a polymath and prolific writer, his works cover a range of topics: *''[[Taj al-'Arus min Jawahir al-Qamus|Tāj al-ʻĀrūs min Jawāhir al-Qāmūs]]'' ["The Bride's Crown from the Pearls of the Dictionary)"]; an expansion of [[Fairuzabadi]]'s ''Al-Qamoos'',{{cite book|first=Elias|last=Muhanna|title=Humanism and Muslim Culture: Historical Heritage and Contemporary Challenges|year=2017|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-17556-0|page=55}} the most frequently cited dictionary of Classical Arabic after ''Lisān al-ʿArab'' by [[Ibn Manẓūr]]. * ''[[Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin|Itḥāf al-Sadāh al-Muttaqīn]]'' ["Presents from Pious Chieftains"], the most comprehensive commentary on [[al-Ghazali]]'s famous [[The Revival of the Religious Sciences|Ihya 'Ulum al-Din]]. It was published in 14 volumes recently and is the second of Zabīdī’s two masterpieces.{{cite book|author=[[Stefan Reichmuth (academic)|Stefan Reichmuth]], [[w:De:Jörn Rüsen|Jörn Rüsen]]|title=Humanism and Muslim Culture: Historical Heritage and Contemporary Challenges|publisher=[[Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht]]|date=2012|isbn=9783899719376|page=121}} * ''[[Asanid al-Kutub as-Sittah|Asānīd al-Kutub as-Sittah]]'' ["The Authentication Chains of the Six Books"]: Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi, Nasayi, Abū Dawud, Ibn Majah are the six motherbooks of Ĥadīth and termed as [[Kutub al-Sittah]]. Zabidi collected the narrators and their chains in this book as is apparent from the title. * ''Úqūd al-Jawāhir al-Munīfah fī Adillati Madh’hab al-Imām Abū Ĥanīfah'' ["Stringing the Blessed Pearls on extract: Al-Murtaḍá al-Husaynī al-Zabīdī (Arabic: المرتضى الحسيني الزبيدي), or Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Murtaḍá al-Zabīdī (1732–1790 / 1145–1205 AH), also known as Murtada al-Zabidi, was an Indian Sunni polymath based in Cairo. He was a Hanafi scholar, hadith specialist, philologist, linguist, lexicographer, genealogist, biographer, historian, mystic and theologian. He was considered one of the leading intellectuals of the 18th century. He was also regarded as the greatest Hadith scholar of his time and one of the foremost philologists of the Arab post-classical era.
